definition: The C character set is the collection of characters that can be used to write C source code. It includes letters, digits, special characters, and white-space characters.
A token is one of the smallest meaningful units in a C program. C programs are built by arranging tokens according to C syntax.
A keyword is a word with a predefined meaning in C. An identifier is a programmer-chosen name for a variable, function, array, or another program element.
An identifier is a name used for a program element. In beginner ANSI C, it should begin with a letter, continue with letters, digits, or underscores, contain no spaces, and must not be a keyword.
A constant is a fixed value that does not change while the program is executing. C uses several kinds of constants, including numeric constants and character-related constants.
A decimal integer constant is a whole-number literal written with decimal digits. It has no decimal point and may have an optional leading sign in an expression.
C can write integer constants in number bases other than decimal. A leading `0` indicates octal notation, while a leading `0x` or `0X` indicates hexadecimal notation.
An integer constant can use suffix letters such as `U`/`u` for unsigned and `L`/`l` for long so the literal is treated with the intended integer category.
A real constant represents a number with a fractional value. In decimal notation it is written with a decimal point and digits before or after the point.
Scientific notation writes a real constant using a mantissa and an exponent separated by `e` or `E`. The exponent tells how many powers of ten scale the mantissa.
A single-character constant represents one character enclosed in single quotation marks, such as `'A'`, `'5'`, or `'x'`.
A string constant is a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks. It can contain letters, numbers, symbols, spaces, and escape sequences.
An escape sequence is a backslash-based character notation used to represent special characters that are difficult to type or would otherwise have a special meaning.
A variable is a data name used to store a value. Unlike a literal constant, the value held by a variable may change while the program runs.
C is case-sensitive, so uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as different. `Total`, `TOTAL`, and `total` can refer to different identifiers.
A data type tells C what kind of data a value represents and guides how the compiler stores and operates on that data.
Integer types store whole numbers. C provides forms such as `short int`, `int`, `long int`, and signed or unsigned versions so programs can choose different integer ranges and representations.
Floating-point types store real-number approximations, including values with fractional parts. C commonly provides `float`, `double`, and `long double`.
`char` is the basic character-sized integer type used for character data, while `void` represents the absence of a value in contexts such as function return types.
A variable declaration introduces one or more variable names to the compiler and specifies the data type they will hold before those variables are used.
`typedef` lets a programmer create another name for an existing data type. The new name can then be used in later declarations.
An enumeration (`enum`) defines a set of named integer constants. The names make related integer choices easier to read and understand.
A storage class helps describe a variable's storage duration, visibility/linkage, or storage suggestion. The book introduces `auto`, `static`, `extern`, and `register` as important storage classes.
Assignment stores a value in a variable. In C the assignment operator `=` puts the value of the right-hand expression into the variable on the left.
Initialization gives a variable its first value as part of its declaration. C also allows several variables to be initialized in one declaration.
`scanf` is a standard input function that can read formatted values from the keyboard/input stream into variables. A control string describes the expected data format.
A symbolic constant gives a meaningful name to a fixed replacement value using the preprocessor directive `#define`. The preprocessor substitutes the replacement text before compilation.
The `const` qualifier tells the compiler that a variable is intended not to be modified through that name after initialization.

The `volatile` qualifier tells the compiler that a variable's value may change for reasons outside the ordinary flow of the current code, so accesses must not be optimized away based on an assumption that the value stays unchanged.

Overflow occurs when a value is outside the representable range of its data type. For floating-point data, underflow describes values whose magnitude is too small to represent normally at the required precision.
